h: Salmon, sea stacks and a short sharp thrill
p: The bridge you walk across today is a modern, well-maintained version, but the idea is centuries old. Fishermen strung a crossing here for generations so they could net the Atlantic salmon that pass close to the island on their way along the coast. The fishery eventually wound down as salmon numbers fell, but you can still see the little whitewashed fisherman's cottage on the island, which gives the place a real sense of the people who once worked it.

The crossing itself only takes a minute or so, and it's roughly 20 metres long with a big drop to the water beneath. Once you're on the island there's a grassy top to explore with views back along the cliffs, so don't feel you have to turn straight round. Look down too: the water around here can be an astonishing shade of turquoise on a bright day.

Strong winds can stop crossings, so have a back-up plan if the forecast looks wild. Give yourself around an hour and a half to two hours in total, including the walk out and back, a pause for photos and a breather on the island.

Right by the car park sits Larrybane, an old quarry with dramatic white chalk cliffs that fans of a certain fantasy TV series will recognise. A few minutes along the coast road, Ballintoy Harbour is a pretty spot for a wander, and Whitepark Bay's sweep of sand is perfect for blowing away the cobwebs. Back in Ballycastle, the harbour is where boats leave for Rathlin Island, which makes a cracking extra day if you're staying in the area.
